newsitem.title: USA: Boise to sell business to Mead for $650 million.
newsitem.headline: Boise to sell business to Mead for $650 million.

text.p: Boise Cascade Corp. has signed a definitive agreement to sell its coated publication paper business to Mead Corp. for about $650 million in cash, the companies said Monday.

The sale, which includes a pulp and paper mill in Rumford, Maine, and 667,000 acres of supporting timberland, is part of Boise Cascade's strategy of narrowing the focus of its paper business to uncoated free sheet and packaging papers.
Uncoated paper is used for commercial printing, envelopes, and business forms and for office applications such as copiers and computer printers.

Separately, Mead said the acquisition will strengthen its position as one of the country's leading producers of a full range of coated papers. The Rumford mill also manufactures high-value speciality paper grades and some commodity grades.
"Coated paper is a targeted growth area for Mead -- we know this segment well, have invested heavily in it, and have been successful," said Steven C. Mason, chairman and chief executive officer.
"The mill complements Mead's two existing coated paper mills, offers important synergies and reinforces Mead's position as high-quality, low-cost producer of value-added paper."
Mead has two other coated paper mills in Escanaba, Mich., and Chillicothe, Ohio. The $5 billion forest products company said the acquisition will boost its 1997 earnings.
Boise Cascade said the sale will "result in a modest gain" that it did not specify.

Boise Cascade said proceeds from the sale will be used to make its remaining paper business more competitive, reduce short-term debt and fund strategic growth in each of the company's three business segments.
The Boise, Idaho-based company also manufactures and distributes office and building products, and owns and manages timberland.

George J. Harad, chairman and chief executive officer of Boise Cascade, said the divestiture will help the company achieve its financial objective of earning a return in excess of its capital cost during each business cycle.
The sale will further increase the significance of distribution in Boise Cascade's overall business mix.
The deal is expected to close by year-end, subject to federal regulatory review.

In 1994, Boise Cascade sold its entire uncoated groundwood paper business and largely exited the newsprint business. Last year, it began to build a new paper machine at its mill in Jackson, Ala., which will be capable of producing 330,000 tons of uncoated free sheet paper annually.

The new machine, scheduled to start up in the spring of 1997, will strengthen Boise Cascade's position as the third-largest manufacturer of uncoated free sheet paper in North America, the company said.

Uncoated free sheet papers are integrated with the company's rapidly growing office products distribution business, Boise Cascade Office Products Corp., who's stock is traded separately on the New York Stock Exchange.
Boise Cascade's stock rose $1.125 to $33.50, while Dayton, Ohio-based Mead was up 75 cents to $59.125 early on the New York Stock Exchange.
